The lower portion of Figure V.11 provides a comparision of auto-to-work trips and total work trips by alternative. The auto travel figures were derived by calculating their 76% share of the total number of trips for each option. Hence, the proportions between options are the same for both auto trips and total trips.
Of the proposed eleven alternatives, areas within walking distance of stations associated with Alternative II generated the highest numbers of auto and total daily work trips in 1970. Alternatives II's greatest numbers are attributable to its additional stations and length in relation to other proposed routings. Station areas of Alternatives I, VI and VII generated only 5% fewer trips, while numbers for Alternatives III, IV and V were respectively 22%, 15% and 37% fewer. Localities proximate to routes of Alternatives VIII and IX generated only about one-third the number of trips that are indicated for Alternative II.
The demographic analysis and the current transit ridership patterns are both indicative of the fact that the proposed rapid transit alternatives would serve areas of high transit dependency and high transit usage. The provision of improved service to transit dependents should expand their range of mobility and enhance their accessibility to health, education, service and shopping facilities as well as potential employment opportunities.

The projection for only a 2.0% gain in jobs in the Regional Core was made without considering the possible effects of a rapid transit system and joint development opportunities. It is likely that a much improved transit system would slow the strong trend toward employment dispersion. Given the structural change occuring in employment in Los Angeles City, i.e., a steady gain in "service industry" jobs which tend to locate in a highly dispersed pattern throughout the region, implementation of a rapid transit system would assist in achieving the 2.0% gain in jobs in the Regional Core. It must be kept in mind that although the Central Business District is projected to increase the number of jobs by 16% by 1990, both Hollywood (-33%) and Wilshire (-15%) are expected to lose jobs. Again, this trend can be slowed or even reversed by provision of a rapid transit system.
